project.name: How Tides Work
project.goal: An educational scroll story explaining ocean tides

typography.heading: Optima, Candara, Segoe UI, Noto Sans, sans-serif
typography.body: system-ui, Segoe UI, Roboto, Ubuntu, sans-serif

content.heading: How Tides Work
content.body: Twice a day the sea rises and falls. Here is why.

accessibility.label: How Tides Work
accessibility.fallbackText: Decorative 3D artwork of a moon over dark water.

content.heading: The Moon pulls on the ocean
content.body: The Moon's gravity pulls hardest on the side of Earth facing it, raising a bulge of water there.

accessibility.label: The Moon pulls on the ocean
accessibility.fallbackText: Abstract decorative artwork of a curved ocean surface.

content.heading: A second bulge on the far side
content.body: On the opposite side, the ocean is pulled less than the planet itself, so a second bulge forms. That is why most coasts see two high tides a day.

accessibility.label: A second bulge on the far side
accessibility.fallbackText: Abstract decorative artwork of two ocean bulges.

content.heading: Earth turns beneath the bulges
content.body: As Earth rotates, a coastline passes through both bulges, about every 12 hours and 25 minutes.

accessibility.label: Earth turns beneath the bulges
accessibility.fallbackText: A slowly turning sphere shown as decorative 3D art.

items.title: New moon
items.text: Sun and Moon line up and their pulls add together: spring tides, with the biggest range.

items.title: First quarter
items.text: They pull at right angles: neap tides, with the smallest range.

items.title: Full moon
items.text: They line up again on opposite sides: spring tides return.

items.title: Last quarter
items.text: Right angles again, and another neap tide.

accessibility.label: Spring and neap tides
accessibility.fallbackText: Four phases of the Moon and their tides.

content.heading: Watch it yourself
content.body: Check a local tide table for a week and compare it with the phase of the Moon.
